source.title: From Perturbation Sensitivity to Sparse Autoencoder Feature Interpretation: An EEG Foundation-Model Case Study
source.authors: Yu-Cong Cao; Chen-Qi Li; Ting-Ting Zhu

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies how to validate physiological interpretations of EEG sparse-autoencoder latents. It does not test whether individual neurons are polysemantic, whether mixed inputs share a feature, or the listed claims about polysemanticity in vision or language models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports original results about perturbation responses and interpretation of SAE latents, included below as findings about a related but different construct. It does not measure individual-neuron responses to unrelated inputs. Comparisons cited from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study trains TopK SAEs on frozen EEG and DINOv3 backbones. It tests whether alpha-perturbation-responsive SAE latents deserve an 'alpha' label. It never measures whether individual neurons respond to unrelated inputs, and does not test superposition, architecture effects or polysemanticity measurement. Its only contact with the claim is a passing citation of monosemanticity work (Bricken et al., Cunningham et al.). It measures SAE-latent interpretation validity, a related but different construct, so its findings go under fits_no_version. The record's 'discusses' overstates the engagement.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that a 7.3× alpha-over-sham SAE response does not survive distortion control, does not mark latents tracking clean alpha in the intended direction, and does not identify readout-important units. They hold that semantic labels need the staged validation ladder.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains TopK SAEs on frozen EEG and cross-modal backbone activations, then tests notch perturbations, distortion normalization, clean-signal correlations, and readout ablations. It does not use the original vision-neuron visualization or SoLU methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The apparent alpha effect changes substantially with the distortion normalization: the pooled ratio is 7.33 raw, 1.32 after time-domain normalization, and 0.28 after spectral-energy normalization. Alpha is the strongest-response band in 15/27 settings, not all settings.

fits_no_version.finding: The raw alpha/sham firing ratio of EEG SAE latents is 7.33. It falls to 1.32 under time-domain normalization and 0.28 under spectral-energy normalization (0/27 settings >1). Alpha-selected latents are slightly anti-correlated with clean relative alpha power (r = −0.073, negative in 23/27 settings), even against activity-matched controls.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perturbation sensitivity alone does not validate a semantic or physiological label for an SAE latent. Intervention-magnitude controls and clean-input validation are required, and conclusions depend on the normalization chosen.

fits_no_version.finding: Alpha selectivity correlates weakly with linear-probe importance (r = 0.107). Zeroing specialist-like groups changes frozen-probe balanced accuracy by +0.0055 (CI spans 0), versus −0.028 for fragile groups and −0.019 for random groups.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Perturbation-defined SAE specialists are not preferentially important to a linear task readout.

record.code_released: An anonymized code archive with training and analysis scripts is provided as supplementary material; URL not stated.
record.problems: The authors note that most settings use one SAE seed; the task-readout analyses cover 21/27 settings; readout groups are unmatched on baseline activity; TopK competition can affect |∆f|; relative band power tests only a global frequency reading; band-stop filtering cannot isolate a biological oscillator; and the two normalization schemes bound rather than eliminate the distortion confound. The work does not test whether any SAE latent represents structured spatial–spectral features or another physiological property.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix C reports channel-dropout robustness by depth, and the six-band sweep includes additional perturbation comparisons. These are omitted because they do not measure the listed polysemanticity versions or add a distinct validation outcome to the rows above.

untested.parts: Image-classifier neurons responding to unrelated visual inputs. DINOv3 is used only as an EEG encoder, and no neuron-level analysis is done.
Share of polysemantic MLP neurons in transformer language models, and how it varies by layer.
Superposition as the cause of polysemanticity. SAEs are used as a tool, but feature packing is not tested.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization or noise without capacity pressure.
How the polysemantic share changes with activation function, architecture or regularization, and at what performance cost.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect one shared feature.

Whether neuron polysemanticity classification depends on activation range or explanation scoring. The paper's normalization-dependence result concerns physiological labels of SAE latents, not neuron polysemanticity.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']; their states describe the alpha-label hypothesis, not any claim version. The connection to V7 is only analogical: measurement-dependence of SAE-latent labels, not of neuron polysemanticity. Appendix C depth-robustness results are irrelevant to the versions.

versions.untested_parts: Image-classifier neurons and mixed responses to unrelated visual inputs.
Transformer language-model MLP neurons and their responses to tokens or contexts.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or feature capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Changes in the share of polysemantic neurons across architectures, activation functions, or regularization.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related subfeatures rather than unrelated inputs.
Whether neuron polysemanticity classifications depend on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.
